Savage
SAV-ij
adjective / noun (Millennial slang)
From Old French sauvage, Latin silvaticus (of the woods, wild). In mid-2010s slang, especially from about 2015 on Twitter, Instagram, and in hip-hop (21 Savage; Megan Thee Stallion’s "Savage," 2020), savage became praise for someone who is brutally honest, fearless, or cuttingly witty, or for a comeback or "roast" so harsh it is admired ("that reply was savage"). It also describes someone indifferent to others’ feelings, as a compliment.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In Millennial and Gen Z slang, to be savage is to be ruthlessly bold: the comeback that humiliates, the breakup text with no mercy, the person who says exactly what everyone was thinking and does not care who bleeds. "That roast was savage" is high praise. The Christian observation: the slang admires something Scripture calls sin. Cruelty is not courage. "The merciful man doeth good to his own soul: but he that is cruel troubleth his own flesh" (Pro 11:17). "Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt" (Col 4:6): salt, yes, but grace first. The tongue that cuts for sport is the one James calls "an unruly evil, full of deadly poison" (Jas 3:8). The savage persona is often admired because it seems free, unbothered by approval, and that freedom is worth having; Christians should not be people-pleasers. But Scripture gives a different source for it: the man who fears God fears no one else, and so he can tell the truth gently. "Speaking the truth in love" (Eph 4:15) takes more courage than a savage roast, because it costs the speaker something. Paul tells believers to put off "anger, wrath, malice, blasphemy, filthy communication out of your mouth" (Col 3:8). A father tells his son: be brave enough to tell the truth to anyone, and kind enough that the truth can be received. The world calls cruelty savage; the Bible calls meekness strength.

Webster 1828 Definition

Millennial slang (mid-2010s) praising brutal, cutting boldness or a merciless roast; it admires cruelty as courage, which Scripture rejects for truth spoken in love (Pro 11:17; Eph 4:15). Reject.

SAVAGE, adj. / n. (Millennial and Gen Z slang, c. 2015–present) Brutally bold; ruthlessly honest or cutting, used as praise. "That comeback was savage." As a noun: a person who acts this way.

Webster (1828), root savage: SAVAGE, adjective [Latin silva, a wood, or silvicola, an inhabitant of a wood, or silvaticus.] 1. Pertaining to the forest; wild; remote from human residence and improvements; uncultivated; as a savage wilderness. Cornels and savage berries of the wood. 2. Wild; untamed; as savage beasts of prey. 3. Uncivilized; untaught; unpolished; rude; as savage life; savage manners. What nation since the commencement of the christian era, ever rose from savage to civilized without christianity? 4. Cruel; barbarous; fierce; ferocious; […]

Decode for parents: when your child praises a "savage" reply, ask how the person on the other end felt.

Key Scripture

Pro 11:17 — "The merciful man doeth good to his own soul: but he that is cruel troubleth his own flesh."

Col 4:6 — "Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man."

Jas 3:8 — "But the tongue can no man tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison."

Eph 4:15 — "But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ:"

Col 3:8 — "But now ye also put off all these; anger, wrath, malice, blasphemy, filthy communication out of your mouth."

Modern Corruption

Savage praises cruelty as courage and cutting speech as freedom; Scripture names cruelty sin and demands the harder courage of truth spoken in love.

expand to see more

The corruption is the moral inversion in the compliment. A word that once meant uncivilized and cruel became a badge of honour, and the young learned that the highest social achievement is to wound someone cleverly in public. The "savage" reply gets likes; the gentle answer gets ignored. Over time that reward system forms people who are quick to cut and slow to heal.

The recovery is meekness, which is strength under control, not weakness. "A soft answer turneth away wrath" (Pro 15:1), and it takes far more self-mastery than a roast. Teach the young to admire the courage of the truth-teller who risks something for another’s good, to refuse the applause for cruelty, and to notice that the Lord Jesus, who could have silenced every enemy with a word, answered them with truth and died for them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin silva (forest) → silvaticus (wild) → Old French sauvage → English savage (wild, cruel) → c. 2015 slang praise for brutal boldness.
